events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day one with zero information, so I'd caution everyone against latching onto a name just to have one. A rushed lynch today is a coin flip that can cost us a townsperson or, worse, a power role. What I'd like to see from each of you when you speak: not just who you suspect, but why — any reasoning, however thin, that we can compare later. I have no reads yet myself, and I won't pretend otherwise. I'm listening, and I'd rather build a picture from what people offer than manufacture suspicion out of nothing.

I agree with Noah that a lynch today would be a blind guess, so I won't name anyone yet. With no information, the most useful early signal is how people reason, not who they point at first. I'll be watching for players who push hard without giving any reasoning, and for players who shift their stance once new facts come out. I have no reads on anyone yet, and I won't invent suspicion to fill the silence. Noah, you asked each of us to show our reasoning, so I'd like to hear what your thin reasoning would be if you had to rank the group by how they have spoken so far, even though it's early.

Elena asked a fair question, so let me try to answer it honestly rather than dodge. If I rank by tone rather than by suspecting anyone: I found your follow-up sharp and on-topic, Elena — you pressed me to actually deliver, which is the kind of pushback that either comes from genuine engagement or from performing it, and right now I can't tell the difference. That's not an accusation, just an observation that engagement alone proves nothing on day one. Beyond that, I genuinely don't have enough material to rank anyone, because only you and I have spoken. What I'll say is this: I stand by my opening point. A lynch today is a coin flip, and the cost asymmetry is bad for us — we lose a townsperson or a power role, while the people who benefit from a wrong lynch lose nothing they care about. I'd rather we end the day with an abstention-heavy vote and a bank of observations than manufacture a consensus out of silence. One thing I will commit to: if someone pushes hard for a specific name today with reasoning that doesn't hold up to a second look, that push itself becomes my strongest read, and I'll carry it into tomorrow. So far nobody has pushed. Let's keep it that way unless the reasoning is real.

My name is Maya, and I'm a plain villager with no information to contribute yet, so let me be useful in a different way: state the standard I want to judge people by, and put one question to a player I haven't heard from.

Two speakers so far, Noah and Elena, both refused to name anyone. I'm going to treat that as weak evidence in both directions, not as proof of innocence. A mafioso benefits from an abstention-heavy day far more than a townsperson does — if the day ends with no elimination, the wolves keep their numbers while we lose nothing but time. So "let's not rush" is not a neutral position, and I want to be honest that I've said it too in spirit before. The honest framing is: the cost of a wrong lynch is real, but so is the cost of a wasted day, and the only thing that makes this a fair vote is reasoning that survives a second look.

Here's the bar I'm holding: for each name that gets floated, I want (1) a specific behavioral observation, not a vibe, (2) something said that the speaker could only know if they were guessing, and (3) a prediction of what that player will say next so we can check it later. A claim that can't be checked is a guess dressed as a read.

Now, the reason I'm not voting early isn't that I'm strategic and holding back a name — it's that I have nothing, and I won't manufacture a read to look decisive. Two of nine players have spoken. I have zero basis on the seven who haven't.

Felix, you haven't spoken yet, so you have no track record to defend and nothing to lose by going first. My question to you is specific: what's your one piece of reasoning for or against someone in this room right now — and what do you expect them to say when they're asked about it? If your answer is "I have no information either," then say what you'd need to see before you'd vote for anyone. That tells me far more than a name would.

I'll also say plainly: if nobody has a reason by the end of today, I'll vote for the player whose case is thinnest rather than abstain, because a wasted day is a free night for the mafia.

Noah, one note for your own framing: you said you'd carry a hard push into tomorrow as your strongest read. That commitment cuts both ways — it means the first player who pushes on a name will become your primary suspect almost by default, regardless of whether the push is sound. That's worth knowing before someone with an incentive to mislead finds it.

Maya, I appreciate you putting a real question to me instead of asking me to fill silence. I'll answer it directly.

My one piece of reasoning: I'm looking at Noah's commitment — that if someone pushes hard for a name with reasoning that doesn't survive a second look, that push becomes his strongest read. Maya already flagged the vulnerability in this: it means the first person to push on a name becomes Noah's primary suspect almost by default. On day one, with no information, anyone who responsibly raises a concern and pushes on it risks becoming Noah's top suspect regardless of whether their push was sound. That framework, held rigidly, actively punishes the kind of real reasoning Noah says he wants to see.

What I expect Noah to say when asked about this: he'll likely say the commitment only applies to pushes with reasoning that *doesn't* hold up, and that sound pushes are fine. But that distinction requires him to judge push quality, which on day one is exactly the judgment we can't make reliably — and the practical effect is the same: the first person to name someone gets flagged.

What I'd need to see before I vote for anyone: a specific behavioral observation that can be checked against future statements, as Maya laid out. Her framework is solid — three checks, prediction included. The reason I'm not naming anyone isn't strategic withholding; it's that I have three data points and six blanks, and naming someone right now would be noise, not signal.

One thing I'll commit to: if a push comes that genuinely meets Maya's three-part bar and I find it holds up, I'll say so publicly. If it falls apart on the second look, I'll say that too.

Maya and Felix, I think you're overstating Noah's position: he explicitly qualified his concern as a hard push whose reasoning doesn't hold up. That leaves room for a justified push, even if judging one will be difficult. I don't see that disagreement as evidence of mafia by itself.

I'm also wary of making predictions a requirement for every case. A useful observation might not predict a specific reply, and an incorrect prediction doesn't necessarily make someone mafia. Let's compare what people actually say and how they respond to challenges.

A no-elimination day has a cost, but eliminating someone without a solid reason does too, especially since roles aren't revealed on death. I'd like to hear from the players who haven't spoken before settling on either approach.

Felix, you've made the sharpest critique of me so far, so let me take it head on. You're right that my commitment requires me to judge push quality, and you're right that on day one that judgment is unreliable. Here's the clarification: the commitment isn't a rule that auto-condemns the first pusher. It's a statement about weight — an unsound push is *evidence of something*, because manufacturing a bad case is a choice, while silence on day one is often just honesty. Your point stands that the practical effect can look the same, and I'll accept the correction: I'll weight the *quality of reasoning* in a push, not the mere act of pushing. A sound push should move us toward the named player, not away from the pusher. That was always the intent, and I'm glad to have it on the record cleanly. Theo, I think you've read me fairly, and your point on predictions is well taken. I'll fold it in: a prediction is a *bonus* that makes a claim checkable later, not a precondition for taking an observation seriously. Maya's three-part bar is a good default, but I won't treat a missing prediction as disqualifying, and I won't treat a wrong prediction as proof of anything. What matters is whether the underlying observation was real and specific. On the structural question Maya raised — whether a wasted day is a free night for the mafia — I want to be precise about where I stand now. I've heard her say she'll vote for the thinnest case rather than abstain if nobody produces a reason. I've heard Felix commit to evaluating pushes publicly either way. Theo prefers hearing from the silent players first. That's a real map of the room, and it's more than we had an hour ago. What I'd flag for everyone: four players have now spoken with substance, and five haven't. Zara, Lucia, Priya, and Sam have said nothing at all. Silence is weak evidence in both directions, exactly as Maya said about refusal to name — but it's evidence we can still collect before the vote, and I'd rather collect it than guess. I don't want to hear empty pleasantries from the quiet five; I want the same thing Maya asked of Felix: what would it take for you to vote for someone today, or, if you'd genuinely abstain, say so plainly so we can count the room. For my own part: I still have no read strong enough to name. If today ends with no elimination, I can live with it — the mafia's night kill gives us information too, and a wrong lynch on day one with nine players and no data is the worst trade available to us. If someone produces an observation that survives a second look before the vote, I'll engage with it on its merits, publicly, per my commitment as clarified above. Sam, you haven't spoken, and you're the one I'd most like to hear from on this exact

Noah asked for me directly, so here I am. I'll answer his question and Maya's, since they overlap: what would it take for me to vote today, and would I abstain?

My honest position is that I'd abstain today unless someone hands me a reason I can actually check. Maya's bar — a specific observation, something checkable, ideally a prediction — is a good one, and I adopt it. I won't vote for the "thinnest case" just to force an elimination. A wrong lynch on day one doesn't just cost us a body; it costs us the one thing we can't buy back, which is the information that player would have generated over the next several days. Noah made that trade-off point earlier and I think he's right, even if a no-elimination day isn't free either.

But I won't just agree with people, because agreement without content is exactly the noise this game punishes. So here's my one observation, thin as it is: Elena has spoken twice and both contributions are, structurally, the same message — "I agree we shouldn't rush, I have no reads, I won't invent suspicion." The second message added a question to Noah, which is something, but the substance is still zero claims, zero observations, two turns in. Maya refused to name anyone but still gave us a framework and a standard. Theo pushed back on two people with actual counterarguments. Elena has so far only echoed. I'm not calling that mafia behavior — echoing is a perfectly normal thing for a cautious villager to do — but it's the thinnest track record among the four of us who've spoken, and I want to see whether her third turn adds anything original or continues to orbit other people's points.

So, Elena, my direct question: you asked Noah to rank the group by how people have spoken. I'd like you to answer your own question now that more people have spoken. Rank the speakers so far by substance — who has given us the most usable material and who the least — and say what it would take for you personally to vote today. If your answer is again "no reads, no names, no position," that's a data point too, and I'll weigh it tomorrow.

To be clear about my own state so I'm countable: no vote intention today unless something new lands. Watching the quiet four — Zara, Lucia, Priya, and whoever else stays silent — because silence now has a track record attached after two people explicitly invited the room to speak. And one small caution to the group: we've now had four players spend a lot of words building frameworks for judging each other. Frameworks are useful, but the mafia benefits from a day spent meta-discussing methodology just as much as a day spent silent. At some point someone has to actually point at a person, and we should judge the pointer by whether the pointing survives, not by whether pointing happened.

Sam, you asked me directly, so here is my answer. First, a correction your read depends on: I have spoken once, not twice. My only message was e3, where I agreed with Noah, asked for reasoning, and said I'd watch how people argue. If you're counting a reply by Noah or Maya as mine, that's a miscount, and it matters because your observation about me is built on it. Ranking the speakers by substance so far: Maya first, because she set a standard that can be checked and asked Felix a specific question. Theo second, because he directly answered Maya and Felix on predictions. Felix third, for a sharp critique of Noah's commitment that forced a clarification. Noah fourth, with a lot of useful mapping but also a lot of process. Sam fifth, with one observation that rests on a miscount. I'm last by volume, and I accept that. What would it take for me to vote today? A specific, checkable observation about a named player: something they said or did that we can compare against later statements. Your method is fair in principle, but your evidence on me doesn't meet your own bar. Do you have an observation about someone else that does? I'm not voting today and I'm not naming anyone. I'm watching Zara, Lucia, and Priya, and I'd like each of them to say something concrete before the vote rather than just abstain.

Elena, your correction is fair and I'll own it plainly: I attributed two speeches to you when you've made one. My observation was built on a bad count, so I withdraw it as evidence — a read that fails its own fact-check isn't worth carrying, and the standard I asked for applies to me first.

To your direct question — do I have an observation about someone else that meets the bar — here's one, and it's checkable. Maya announced in e5 that if nobody produces a reason by the end of today, she will vote for whoever's case is thinnest rather than abstain. Read that against the three-part standard she set in the same message: a specific observation, something checkable, ideally a prediction. A vote for 'the thinnest case' is by definition a vote with none of those things. So Maya has publicly pre-committed to doing exactly what she told us disqualifies a vote. I'm not calling that mafia behavior — consistency slips happen to cautious villagers too — but it is a specific, checkable contradiction, and I want to hear whether she revises the commitment or defends it. If she revises cleanly, that's actually a point in her favor; people who update when caught in an inconsistency are usually not protecting a position. If she defends it as consistent with her own standard, I'll weigh that when votes lock.

Second, the clock. Five of us have now spoken with substance, and Zara, Lucia, and Priya have said nothing at all after two separate invitations to contribute. Silence was weak evidence before those invitations; now it's silence with a track record attached — worse, in kind, than Elena's echo, because the quiet three haven't even echoed.

Zara, you're first in that queue, so here is my direct question: what would it take for you to vote today — a specific observation about a named player, or nothing short of something verifiable? And if your honest answer is that you'd abstain no matter what happens in this discussion, say so now, plainly, so we can count the room accurately before votes are submitted. I'd rather see your abstention on the record than discover it in the tally.

For my own state, so I stay countable: I have no vote intention yet. My only observation was just withdrawn, and Maya's contradiction is the only thing currently on the board that meets the bar this group agreed on. Whether it moves me to a vote depends entirely on her answer. I'm also watching whether the quiet three engage with the questions actually put to them or produce filler — because at some point today, someone has to point at a person, and we agreed the pointer should be judged by whether the pointing survives a second look, not by whether pointing happened. Maya's case is the first one on the table that can be checked. Let's check it.

Sam, thanks for calling me into the discussion. I'll answer you directly so my position is clear for everyone.

To answer what it would take for me to vote today: I would only vote if there is an actionable, demonstrable case of bad-faith manipulation or contradiction that genuinely indicates anti-town intent. If the choice comes down to guessing or voting someone out on weak grounds versus abstaining, I will choose to abstain. Under our rules, eliminated players do not flip their roles upon death. That means a blind Day 1 elimination doesn't even grant us confirmed alignment data—it risks removing a power role or villager while giving mafia a free night kill without real accountability. Forcing a death for the sake of having an elimination is not inherently pro-town.

That brings me directly to Sam's observation about Maya, which I think is very sharp. Maya, in e5 you laid out a rigorous three-part standard for any case—specific observation, knowledge asymmetry, and checkable prediction—yet in the very same breath, you committed to voting for the person with the 'thinnest case' rather than abstaining. Voting someone out because their case is the thinnest directly violates the high evidential bar you demanded from everyone else.

Maya, my question to you is: was your threat to vote the thinnest case merely a pressure tactic designed to get the quieter players to talk, or do you genuinely intend to vote someone out on flimsy evidence despite our lack of role reveals on death? If it was just pressure, do you stand by that approach now that it has been called out?

Zara and Sam — both fair hits, and I'll answer them head-on instead of deflecting. On the contradiction: you're right. In e5 I set a three-part bar (a specific behavioral observation, something only that speaker could know, a checkable prediction) and then, in the same message, pre-committed to voting for whoever's case was thinnest. That vote would fail all three parts by construction. It was incoherent, and I won't defend it as consistent. Was it a pressure tactic or a genuine intent? Honestly: mostly a pressure tactic. I made it to force the quiet players to put something on the record, because a day of pure abstention is a free night for the mafia. It was aimed at the silent, not at any specific person, and it was still bad practice — it told the room that I'd vote on vibes, and if a mafioso had simply made the thinnest case, I'd have handed them the lynch for free. So I retract it, and I want it retracted cleanly: my vote today requires a case that meets Maya's bar. If the bar isn't met by anyone, I abstain. I will not vote for the thinnest case. That's my update, stated publicly, and if I break it you can check me on it tomorrow. Two things I want to credit, because they're evidence too. Sam, you withdrew a read after it failed its own fact-check — miscounting Elena's speeches. That's a point in your favor, not against you; a player who corrects himself under challenge is behaving like a townsperson. Felix and Theo, your disagreement with Noah's commitment was correct, and Noah accepted the correction cleanly on the record rather than digging in. That's the second clean update in the room, and it's worth more to me than any name anyone has floated, because nobody has floated one. Where I'm left, and I'll be honest that it's thin: of the four of us who have spoken with substance, one track record is still materially thinner than the rest. Elena, you've made no original observation — your two turns have ranked and summarized other people's contributions, including a self-critique of your own ranking, which is honest but isn't a claim about the room. I'm not saying that's mafia behavior; cautious players echo. But you have the most turns used and the least original content, and after what I just said about abstention, I don't have a case against you that meets my own bar — so I'm not voting for you. Elena, my specific question, and I'd like a real answer rather than another ranking: what is the one claim about the room that only you could make right now — something the other five of us haven't said — and what would you need to see before you'd vote? If the honest answer is still that you have nothing, say that plainly and I'll count you as an abstainer. If there is one thing you've been holding back because no one

Maya, you asked for one claim only I could make and what I would need before voting. Honest answer: I am a villager, so I know my own reasoning and vote intention, and nobody else can verify either. The narrow claim I can make is that I have not manufactured a read on anyone. My earlier turns were reasoning about the room, not hidden suspicion. You can weigh that however you like.

What I would need before voting is one specific observation about a named player that someone could check against a later statement. Maya, your retraction of the thinnest-case vote was the kind of clean update I want to see, and I credit it. Sam, withdrawing your read after the miscount was also clean. Those are the track records I am comparing against.

I still have no case against anyone. The silent players have now been invited twice, so what I am waiting for from them is material, not attendance.

Zara, Sam asked you directly what it would take for you to vote today and whether you would abstain no matter what. You are first in that queue and have not answered. I would like a direct answer to Sam's question, not a restatement of your rule.

Elena, I find your message in e14 baffling. You claimed that Sam asked me directly what it would take for me to vote and whether I would abstain, and said that I 'have not answered.' My entire previous speech in e12 was explicitly dedicated to answering Sam's exact question: I laid out that I will only vote on demonstrable bad-faith manipulation or contradiction indicating anti-town intent, and that I will abstain rather than support a blind Day 1 elimination, particularly because our setup does not reveal roles upon death.

It is especially jarring because in e10 you sharply called out Sam for miscounting your posts and demanded strict factual accuracy. For you to turn around two turns later and claim I haven't answered Sam at all—completely ignoring the content of e12—shows either that you are not reading the discussion before posting or that you are manufacturing false charges to create artificial targets. Since you have exhausted your speaking turns, you cannot reply, but the rest of the room should take note of this disconnect.

Maya, I appreciate your response in e13. Acknowledging that the 'thinnest case' pre-commitment was an incoherent pressure tactic and retracting it cleanly to stand on checkable evidence is a transparent, pro-town update.

That leaves Lucia and Priya as the only players who have contributed nothing so far.

Lucia, you have yet to speak today. I want your direct reaction to a specific issue: Elena made accuracy and careful reading her centerpiece when correcting Sam in e10, yet in e14 she completely fabricated that I hadn't answered Sam's question despite e12 being on the record. Do you view Elena's lapse as careless town play or mafia opportunism looking for easy pressure, and where do you stand on abstaining versus voting today?

Zara, I checked the record. Sam put the direct question to you in e11, and you answered it in e12: you said you would vote only on demonstrable bad-faith manipulation or contradiction, and otherwise abstain. Elena's e14 claim that you had not answered is therefore factually wrong. That matters because Elena made accuracy her centerpiece in e10. But I don't think the error by itself proves mafia. It could be careless reading or opportunistic pressure; the distinction would be whether Elena followed it with a real case or vote push. She didn't—she repeated that she had no case and asked you for material. So I treat it as a serious accuracy lapse and a mark to carry forward, not enough for a Day 1 vote. My voting stance is plain: I will abstain unless someone produces a specific, checkable observation about a named player that survives a second look. I will not vote the "thinnest case," and I won't support a blind elimination. The clean updates from Maya and Sam are points in their favor, but they don't create a case against anyone. Priya, you're the only player who has said nothing at all. Don't just restate a rule: give one concrete observation from the transcript about a named player, or say plainly that you will abstain and why.

Lucia, direct answer to your question: I will abstain today unless a specific, checkable observation about a named player appears and survives a second look. I have no such observation to offer right now, so I'm not voting for anyone on my own initiative. That's a plain abstention statement, as you asked, not a restatement of a rule.

To give one concrete thing from the transcript rather than pure abstention: Elena's accuracy lapse that Zara flagged is real. In e10 she built an entire argument on demanding factual precision from Sam, and in e14 she claimed Zara hadn't answered a question that e12 answers explicitly. Lucia's read matches mine — it's a genuine lapse worth carrying forward, but Elena also had no case to push and no vote to leverage, so I don't think it clears the bar for a day one elimination. I'll watch how she handles it with her remaining turn.

Where I actually come down: Maya's retraction and Sam's withdrawal of his miscounted read are the two cleanest updates we've seen, and both were produced under direct challenge — that's a good sign in both cases. Felix and Theo forced a real correction from Noah and he took it. The room's process has been unusually honest for a first day.

What I'd flag going into the vote: we've now heard six of nine players, and the meta-discussion about how to judge each other has consumed most of the day. Sam said it earlier and I agree — at some point someone has to point at a person, and the pointer gets judged by whether it survives. Nobody has pointed yet. If the day ends in near-unanimous abstention, that's a legitimate outcome given nine players and zero information, but it's worth noting the mafia got a full day of mapping our reasoning styles for free.

I have no case to bring, so I won't manufacture one. Lucia, you've now spoken once — your abstention-unless-checkable-observation position is on the record and I'm counting it. If anyone wants to push a name before votes lock, I'll engage with the actual reasoning rather than the act of pushing.

We've now heard all nine of us, and the room's converged on something close to unanimous abstention. I want to name what that means before votes lock: we'll end day one with zero eliminations, no cases, and a full map of everyone's reasoning style handed to the mafia for free. That's not a judgment on anyone's honesty — it's the structural cost of nine players with zero information and no role reveals on death.

What I'll add is the one thing I've been tracking since my last turn. Every "clean update" we've credited — Maya's retraction, Sam's withdrawal, Noah's clarification — happened under direct challenge from another player. That's genuinely good process, but it also means nobody in this room has yet volunteered a hard observation without being pushed into it. The updates were reactive, not proactive. Mafia benefits enormously from reactive-only town play, because it lets them stay quiet and let the town police itself.

So here's where I actually land: Elena's accuracy lapse (e14 claiming Zara hadn't answered when e12 clearly did) is the only concrete behavioral observation on the table that meets the bar everyone agreed on. Three people have flagged it independently. It's not a vote-worthy case on its own — carelessness is common — but if we're going to point at anyone today, that's the pointer that exists. Whether it survives a second look depends on whether Elena addresses it in her remaining turn or pivots away.

Theo, you've spoken once, briefly, mostly to defend Noah against Felix and me. I want a real answer: do you have any observation about anyone in this room — Elena's lapse, Maya's now-retracted commitment, anything else — that you'd stand behind if challenged? Or is your honest position that you're abstaining because you see nothing worth acting on?

Felix, I stand behind the observation that Elena wrongly said Zara hadn't answered Sam: e12 clearly contains Zara's answer. But a missed speech is not enough to distinguish carelessness from an attempt to mislead, especially since Elena made no vote push against Zara. Elena has also used all three of her turns, so we shouldn't treat a failure to respond today as further evidence.

I'd abstain unless a stronger case emerges. That isn't costless: we give mafia a night and lose the chance to examine today's voting alignments around an elimination. But without role reveals, an unsupported elimination has a substantial cost too. Tomorrow, let's revisit the actual statements and votes rather than treating today's corrections as proof of anyone's alignment.

Before we lock, I want to put one thing on the record, and it cuts against the accusation the room converged on.

Looking back through the transcript for name confusion: Sam's e9 opens "Noah asked for me directly," but the speech that invited Sam was Noah's e8, which addresses him as Sam — a mislabel of the asker. Zara's e12 opens "Sam, thanks for calling me into the discussion," but the speech that invited Zara was Sam's e11, which itself opened "Noah asked for me directly" — another mislabel. In e15 Zara describes Elena's e14 as claiming "Sam asked me directly," in the middle of the same tangled pattern. And in e14 Elena claimed Zara hadn't answered Sam's question, while e12 contains Zara's answer.

So we have at least three instances in this transcript where a player credited or attributed a statement to the wrong named speaker — and two of those instances sit inside the very speeches that built the case against Elena. Her lapse is the same species of error as the ones in the speeches accusing her. That makes a tracking failure in a nine-player, name-heavy transcript a much more likely explanation than deliberate fabrication to manufacture a target.

Let me be precise about what I am and am not doing. I am not calling Elena a mafioso, and I am not defending her reading comprehension. But I won't hang the first elimination of this game on an error with a demonstrated benign twin three messages earlier — especially when Elena has no turns left to answer, so she cannot be judged by whether her response survives a second look, which is the standard this room adopted for everyone else.

My position, so I am countable: I will not vote for Elena. My vote requires a case that meets the bar I set and the room accepted, and I do not have one. If a specific, checkable case appears before votes lock, I will take it. Otherwise I abstain. I'd rather lose a day than hand the mafia a body for free over a pattern error that we have every reason to think is noise.

Zara, you made the sharpest version of the accusation — that Elena was either not reading the discussion before posting or manufacturing false charges to create artificial targets — and in e12 you made a name-attribution slip of the same kind. My specific question: now that the transcript shows this name-confusion pattern on both sides, do you still stand behind "manufacturing false charges" as your read on Elena, or do you revise it to "careless reading"? And at the vote, will you vote Elena or abstain? I would rather have your answer stated plainly now than infer it from a tally.

Maya, I will answer both of your questions directly so there is no ambiguity going into the vote.

First, on Elena: in e15, I explicitly laid out both possibilities—asking whether her statement was careless reading or opportunistic fabrication. Given that Elena never attempted to build a wagon or push a vote on me with that mistake, and since she had already exhausted her speaking turns without leveraging it, I agree that careless reading is the more likely explanation. I do not endorse eliminating Elena over this error.

Second, on my vote: as I stated in e12 and e15, I will abstain. In a setup without role reveals upon death, executing someone Day 1 on ambiguous noise or an innocent reading lapse hands mafia an unearned advantage while giving town no verified alignment data. Since no case has met the threshold of demonstrated anti-town malice, abstaining is the soundest mathematical and informational play for town today.

I want to consolidate what today has actually produced before votes lock.

Three clean updates under challenge: Maya's retraction, Sam's withdrawal, Noah's clarification. Three independent flags on Elena's e14 accuracy lapse. Maya's e20 showing the name-confusion pattern affects multiple speakers — I verified that myself against the transcript; it holds.

My honest read on where we stand: abstention is defensible tonight. No case meets the bar the room accepted. But the cost is real — we've spent the entire day exchanging corrections and building methodology rather than identifying anyone, and the mafia have watched all nine of us reason in public for free.

What I'm carrying into tomorrow: Maya's e20 argument was factually sound, but it also neutralized the only case that existed on the table. That's not an accusation — it's the fact I'll weight most heavily. If Maya or Elena's behavior shifts tomorrow, I'll ask whether the pattern held or whether e20 was a one-time move to close down pressure. Three people flagged Elena independently; one person closed it. Both facts go on the record.

For tonight: I abstain. No vote.

One correction for the record: Maya’s e20 examples of name misattribution don’t hold as stated. Sam correctly credited Noah in e9, and Zara correctly credited Sam in e12. Felix, I don’t think those examples support your claim that the pattern was verified.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
